Failure modes include storage quota exhaustion, checksum mismatches during transfer, and partial write failures due to disk errors. The design preserves already captured history by creating immutable snapshots of every raw object with full metadata including creation timestamps and access logs, ensuring that any previously preserved data can be exactly reproduced from the ledger without any loss or alteration of original captured raw content.

## Masking
The masking interface applies selective redaction and anonymization to sensitive data fields while maintaining structural integrity of the data envelope. It defines rules for field-level masking based on data types and sensitivity tags. Failure modes include over-masking leading to data loss, under-masking causing leakage, and rule conflicts during complex transformations. Concrete verification examples involve processing sample datasets with known sensitive fields, applying masks, and validating that non-sensitive content remains unchanged while masked fields are replaced with placeholders. The design preserves already captured history by recording the exact masking rules applied at each step in an immutable audit trail, allowing full reconstruction of masked versions of any historical data snapshot without exposing or altering the original captured information.

## Reader Order
The reader order interface enforces sequential processing of incoming events or messages using priority queues and ordering guarantees. It tracks consumer positions and handles reordering during backpressure. Failure modes include queue overflows causing dropped messages, out-of-order delivery due to network reordering, and starvation of low-priority readers. Concrete verification examples test message ordering with injected delays and reordering, confirming that all messages are delivered in the expected sequence with correct consumer offsets. The design preserves already captured history by persisting the full event stream with sequence numbers and timestamps in an append-only log, enabling exact replay of any past reader state to verify ordering invariants over time.

## Search Indexing
The search indexing interface maintains inverted indexes and full-text search capabilities over stored components with support for incremental updates. It provides query APIs with relevance scoring and facet filtering. Failure modes include index corruption during rebuilds, stale index versions due to lag, and query timeouts on large datasets. Concrete verification examples involve building indexes on historical datasets, running test queries that match known terms, and simulating index rebuilds to confirm that search results remain consistent. The design preserves already captured history by versioning every index update and storing the complete index state at each commit point, allowing deterministic reconstruction of any previous search index configuration and results.

## Atomic Publication
The atomic publication interface ensures that published changes are committed atomically across multiple stores with rollback on any failure. It coordinates prepare and commit phases for distributed publication. Failure modes include partial commit states, network partitions during two-phase commit, and deadlock in locking. Concrete verification examples test publication of multi-component updates under simulated failures, verifying that either all changes are published or none are left in inconsistent state. The design preserves already captured history by recording the full pre-publish state and post-publish state in paired immutable logs, ensuring that any historical publication attempt can be exactly replayed or rolled back using the preserved ledger entries.

## Crash Recovery
The crash recovery interface implements logging and replay mechanisms for state restoration after system failures. It tracks operation logs and recovery checkpoints. Failure modes include incomplete log writes during crashes, loss of checkpoint data, and replay loops from corrupted logs. Concrete verification examples simulate power loss mid-operation and confirm that the system recovers to the last consistent state with all logged operations reapplied correctly. The design preserves already captured history by maintaining separate immutable recovery logs that capture every operation and checkpoint, allowing exact restoration of any previously captured state even after multiple crash events.

## Cancellation
The cancellation interface provides graceful handling of long-running operations that can be interrupted by user or system signals. It propagates cancellation tokens through the call stack. Failure modes include ignored cancellations leading to zombie processes, race conditions during cancellation, and partial state cleanup. Concrete verification examples test cancellation during simulated long computations, confirming that resources are released promptly and no partial results are left behind. The design preserves already captured history by logging every cancellation event with full context and final state, enabling replay of the exact cancellation sequence that occurred at any point in time.

## Bounded Memory
The bounded memory interface manages memory usage through paging, eviction policies, and size limits on cached data. It enforces hard limits and garbage collection triggers. Failure modes include thrashing under high load, memory leaks from untracked allocations, and eviction of hot data. Concrete verification examples monitor memory footprint during large dataset processing and verify that the adapter correctly evicts least recently used items while maintaining correctness of remaining data. The design preserves already captured history by checkpointing memory-resident state to disk at regular intervals and recording all eviction decisions, allowing full restoration of any previously captured memory state from the immutable log.
